hmmt-feb-2008-geo-01.title: Classify the triangles
hmmt-feb-2008-geo-01.body:
In a unit cube the triangles formed by three vertices have side lengths $(1,1,\sqrt2)$, $(1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ or $(\sqrt2,\sqrt2,\sqrt2)$.
- $(1,1,\sqrt2)$: angles $45^\circ,45^\circ,90^\circ$.
- $(1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ (right triangle): angles $90^\circ$, $\arcsin\frac1{\sqrt3}\approx35.26^\circ$, $\arcsin\sqrt{\frac23}\approx54.74^\circ$.
- equilateral: $60^\circ$.

The distinct values are $45^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $35.26^\circ$, $54.74^\circ$, $60^\circ$: $5$ values.

**Answer: 5**

hmmt-feb-2008-geo-02.title: Distances along the altitude
hmmt-feb-2008-geo-02.body:
Both centers lie on the altitude from $A$. A circle of radius $\rho$ tangent to both $AB$ and $AC$ has its center at distance $\rho/\sin30^\circ=2\rho$ from $A$. With radii $r$ ($\Omega$) and $\rho$ ($\omega$): $A\Omega=2r$, $A\omega=2\rho$, and external tangency (with $\omega$ closer to $A$) gives $2r-2\rho=r+\rho$, so $r=3\rho$.

**Answer: 3**

hmmt-feb-2008-geo-03.title: Coordinates
hmmt-feb-2008-geo-03.body:
Let $A=(0,0)$. The circle touching both legs has center $O=(r,r)$ and the points opposite the tangency points are $X'=(r,2r)$ and $Y'=(2r,r)$, which lie on $BC$. Since $A=(0,0)$ and the legs are the axes, $BC$ has equation $x+y=c$ for $c=AB=AC$ (the triangle is isosceles because $\angle X'OY'=90^\circ$ with $X'=(r,2r)$, $Y'=(2r,r)$ on $BC$ forces slope $-1$). Thus $3r=c=6$, $r=2$.

The part of the circle beyond $BC$ is the circular segment cut off by chord $X'Y'$, where $\angle X'OY'=90^\circ$: area $=\frac14\pi r^2-\frac12r^2=\pi-2$.

**Answer: $\pi-2$**

hmmt-feb-2008-geo-04.title: Congruent circles give an isosceles triangle
hmmt-feb-2008-geo-04.body:
The chord $AD$ has the same length in both congruent circles, so it subtends equal inscribed angles: $\angle ABD=\angle ACD$. Hence $AB=AC$.

Let $M$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$, the midpoint of $BC=18$. Then $MC=9$, $MD=9-4=5$, and $AM=\sqrt{13^2-5^2}=12$. Area $=\frac12\cdot18\cdot12=108$.

**Answer: 108**

hmmt-feb-2008-geo-05.title: The hole is a kite
hmmt-feb-2008-geo-05.body:
Folding a sheet of paper this way shows that the hole is a kite $ABCD$ symmetric about the first fold line $AC$ (with $B$ the mirror image of $D$), and the second fold line makes angle $\varphi=\angle CAD+\angle ADE$, where the cut through $D$ is such that $\angle ADE=\angle CDE$ (side $DC$ folded onto $DA$).

The center $O$ with $\angle XOY=144^\circ$ and all other vertices on a circle about $O$ must be $A$ or $C$ (the vertices where $\angle XOY$ is between two equal sides).

- If $O=A$: $\angle BAD=144^\circ$, so $\angle CAD=72^\circ$, and since $AC=AD$, $\angle ACD=\angle ADC=54^\circ$, $\angle ADE=27^\circ$, giving $\varphi=72^\circ+27^\circ=99^\circ$, not allowed since $\varphi<90^\circ$.
- If $O=C$: $\angle ACD=72^\circ$ is half of $144^\circ$; $CA=CD$ gives $\angle CAD=\angle CDA=54^\circ$, $\angle ADE=27^\circ$, so $\varphi=54^\circ+27^\circ=81^\circ$.

**Answer: $81^\circ$**

hmmt-feb-2008-geo-06.title: Power of a point
hmmt-feb-2008-geo-06.body:
By the extended law of sines, $R=\frac{BC}{2\sin A}=\frac{8}{\sqrt2}=4\sqrt2$. The power of $P$ with respect to the circumcircle gives $R^2-OP^2=PB\cdot PC=15$, so $OP^2=32-15=17$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{17}$**

hmmt-feb-2008-geo-07.title: Radical center
hmmt-feb-2008-geo-07.body:
Let $D$ be the tangency point of $C_1$ and $C_2$. $T$ has equal tangent lengths $TA=TB$ to $C_1$... ($TA$ is also tangent to $C_1$ at $A$, $TB$ to $C_2$), so $T$ lies on the radical axis of $C_1$, $C_2$, which is their common tangent at $D$. Thus $TD=TA=4$.

Now $\tan\frac{\angle ATD}2=\frac{2}{TD}=\frac12$ and $\tan\frac{\angle BTD}2=\frac3{TD}=\frac34$. The radius of $C_3$ is $TA\tan\frac{\angle ATB}2=4\tan\left(\frac{\angle ATD}2+\frac{\angle BTD}2\right)=4\cdot\frac{\frac12+\frac34}{1-\frac12\cdot\frac34}=4\cdot2=8$.

**Answer: 8**

hmmt-feb-2008-geo-08.title: Unfold by reflections
hmmt-feb-2008-geo-08.body:
Suppose the path meets $AB$, $BC$, $CA$ in this order. Reflect $C$ over $AB$ to get $C'$, then reflect $A$ over $BC'$ to get $A'$, then $B$ over $A'C'$ to get $B'$. Unfolding the path by successively reflecting the remainder across the sides it hits, it becomes a straight segment from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$, the image of $\Gamma$ under the three reflections, a circle of radius $\frac12$ centered at the center of $A'B'C'$.

The centers of $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ are $\sqrt{3^2+\left(\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^2}=\sqrt{\frac{28}3}$ apart, so the shortest path between the circles has length $\sqrt{\frac{28}3}-\frac12-\frac12=\sqrt{\frac{28}3}-1$. Reflecting it back gives a valid path in $ABC$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{\frac{28}{3}}-1$**

hmmt-feb-2008-geo-09.title: Collinearity and power of a point
hmmt-feb-2008-geo-09.body:
Let the incircle touch $AC,AB$ at $E,F$. Both lie on the circle with diameter $AI$ (right angles at $E,F$). Claim: $D,E,P$ are collinear and $D,F,Q$ are collinear (angle chase: $\angle PEA=\angle PIA=\angle IBA+\angle IAB=90^\circ-\frac C2=\angle DEC$).

Then the power of $D$ with respect to the circle $AEIF$ gives $DE\cdot DP=DF\cdot DQ$, so $\frac{DP}{DQ}=\frac{DF}{DE}$.

$DF=2DB\sin\angle DBI$ with $DB=\sqrt{36-9}=3\sqrt3$, $\sin\angle DBI=\frac36$: $DF=3\sqrt3$. $DE=2DC\sin\angle DCI$ with $DC=\sqrt{25-9}=4$, $\sin\angle DCI=\frac35$: $DE=\frac{24}5$. So $\frac{DF}{DE}=\frac{5\sqrt3}8$ and $\left(\frac{DP}{DQ}\right)^2=\frac{75}{64}$.

**Answer: $\frac{75}{64}$**

hmmt-feb-2008-geo-10.title: Poles and harmonic division
hmmt-feb-2008-geo-10.body:
Let $AD$ meet $\omega$ again at $H$. Since $AE,AF$ are tangents and $ADH$ a secant, $DEHF$ is a harmonic quadrilateral, so the pole of line $AD$ lies on $EF$. The pole of $AD$ also lies on $\ell$ (the line through $O$ perpendicular to $AD$). Hence the pole of $AD$ is $G$, and $GD$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $D$, i.e. $G$ lies on line $BC$.

The pencil $(AE,AF;AD,AG)$ is harmonic, so intersecting with $BC$, $(C,B;D,G)$ is harmonic. With $s=3012$: $BD=s-AB=1003$, $CD=s-AC=1004$ (the excircle opposite $A$ touches $BC$ at distance $s-c$ from $B$). Put $DG=x$ with $G$ beyond $B$ (since $BD<CD$, $G$ is on the $B$ side): $\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{BG}{CG}$ i.e. $\frac{1003}{1004}=\frac{x-1003}{x+1004}$, giving $1003x+1003\cdot1004=1004x-1003\cdot1004$, so $x=2\cdot1003\cdot1004=2014024$.

**Answer: 2014024**
